name: Raghu
definition: Raghu is a composite portrait of a private bus driver navigating the Puttur-Mangaluru route in Dakshina Kannada district, balancing household expenses against the pressures of an intensely competitive stage-carriage market. He embodies the economic realities of a working family in the coastal belt where literacy is high but schooling expenses, occupational uncertainty and Gulf-migration patterns reshape children's educational trajectories.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raghu drives a private stage-carriage bus on the Puttur-Mangaluru route six days a week, beginning his shift at four-thirty in the morning and finishing after eight in the evening. He earns around sixteen thousand rupees monthly as salary plus a small share of the daily collection, which fluctuates with passenger numbers and petrol prices. The Shakti free-bus scheme for women has cut his operator's revenue sharply since it began, forcing management to run fewer trips and demand faster turnarounds. Raghu eats breakfast at a roadside hotel in Kabaka, packs lunch from home and takes his evening meal at a friend's tea-shop near the Pumpwell junction in Mangaluru. His knees ache from the clutch, his eyes burn from the glare off the NH-66 tarmac and he has developed chronic acid reflux, treated with over-the-counter antacids he buys at the petrol-bunk pharmacy. He holds a commercial driving licence renewed every three years and has worked this route for seventeen years, first as a conductor, then passing his heavy-vehicle test in 2012. Debt from a failed arecanut-plantation venture a decade ago still constrains the household budget.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raghu lives with his wife Sharada, their two sons aged nineteen and fifteen, and his widowed mother in a modest tiled house on the edge of Puttur town, within walking distance of the bus stand. Sharada works part-time as an assistant in a private Kannada-medium primary school, earning about four thousand rupees monthly, which covers groceries and the younger son's tuition fees. Their elder son Kiran completed his second-year pre-university at a government college in Puttur but left in mid-year to take up work at a Gulf-recruitment agency in Mangaluru, preparing documents and translating for Beary-speaking applicants; the family hopes he will eventually secure his own Gulf posting through the contacts he is building. The younger boy Tejas studies in Class 10 at a Kannada-medium government high school and is a good student, regularly scoring above seventy percent, but the family worries about affording private pre-university tuition if he passes his SSLC this year. Raghu's mother, now seventy-one, manages the household kitchen and receives a small widow's pension. Sharada's earnings, though modest, give her a say in decisions about the boys' futures, and she insists Tejas should finish his studies before thinking of work.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raghu himself studied only up to Class 7 in a village school near Sullia taluk before his father's ill-health forced him to begin working as a conductor at seventeen. Sharada completed her SSLC and worked in a garment unit before marriage, and her schooling opened the door to her current school job. Kiran attended the same government high school where Tejas now studies, scoring sixty-eight percent in his SSLC and gaining admission to the commerce stream at the government pre-university college; the family paid nothing for his high-school years apart from textbooks and uniform, but college brought expenses for bus fare, notebooks and private coaching in accountancy, totalling roughly three thousand rupees a term. When Kiran left college mid-way, Raghu was disappointed but accepted it as practical: the recruitment-agency job pays eight thousand rupees monthly now and promises a Gulf opening within two years, and the household cannot afford to keep an earning-age son dependent. Tejas wants to study science and become a lab technician, but private pre-university colleges charge fifteen to twenty thousand rupees yearly and government seats are fiercely competitive; the family has not yet decided whether they can afford the full two years or whether Tejas too will need to find work after his SSLC.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Raghu's chronic reflux and knee pain, left untreated apart from painkillers, limit his ability to work past fifty, a worry he does not voice openly. He attends the government community health centre in Puttur for minor ailments but travelled to a private clinic in Mangaluru last year when severe abdominal pain frightened the family; the consultation, ultrasound and medicines cost nearly four thousand rupees, wiped out by a loan from his bus-owner. Sharada developed anaemia two years ago and takes iron tablets supplied free at her school's health camp, organised under a district nutrition programme. Raghu's mother has mild diabetes, managed with subsidised Metformin from the Jan Aushadhi pharmacy and careful diet; a cataract is forming in her right eye but surgery will wait until the household can afford the five thousand rupees the government hospital in Mangaluru will charge for lens and post-operative care under Ayushman Bharat. The family is enrolled under the Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka scheme, which would cover hospitalisation, but Raghu fears losing workdays more than the cost itself. Tejas had dengue during the monsoon two years ago, treated at home with paracetamol and oral rehydration, and recovered without hospital admission. No one in the household drinks heavily, but Raghu smokes four or five beedis daily, a habit Sharada criticises quietly.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: The family belongs to the Billava community, historically associated with toddy-tapping but now widely present in transport, small trade and labour across Dakshina Kannada. Raghu's household does not tap toddy, and he describes himself simply as a driver, but he remains proud of the community's Koti-Chennaya epic and its message of defiance against injustice. The family observes Deepavali, Ugadi and Dasara, and Sharada participates in a neighbourhood women's group organised by SKDRDP, Dharmasthala's self-help-group wing, saving fifty rupees weekly toward emergency expenses. They visit the Kudupu Sri Anantha Padmanabha Temple on important occasions and attended a Bhuta Kola performance at a relative's compound near Uppinangady two years ago, an all-night event Raghu remembers vividly for the possessed dancer's leaps and the beat of the drums. Raghu's late father had taken him as a child to the Kukke Subrahmanya Temple, a memory he holds dear. The family speaks Tulu at home, Kannada in school and work, and a little Beary-influenced Dakshina Kannada Kannada when dealing with Muslim traders in Mangaluru. Caste does not dominate daily conversation, but Raghu is aware that Bunts and Brahmins still hold most land and that his own family's economic mobility depends on wages, not property.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has little direct contact with the gram panchayat, as his house lies on the town's edge under the Town Municipal Council's jurisdiction, but Sharada's school receives government mid-day-meal supplies and textbooks, which she says arrive mostly on time. Raghu applied for a Below Poverty Line card three years ago but was refused; the family now holds a yellow ration card and buys subsidised rice and kerosene monthly. He has never used MGNREGA, as his driving work precludes the hundred-day rural-labour guarantee. The household electricity bill under the Gruha Jyoti scheme is now zero up to two hundred units, a significant saving. Raghu deeply resents the new toll plaza on the Mangaluru highway, which forces his operator to pay daily and cuts further into revenue. He believes local MLAs care only about Mangaluru city and ignore Puttur's crumbling bus-stand and potholed approach roads. When the KSRTC raised its fares two years ago, he joined a one-day private-operators' strike, the only political action he has taken beyond voting.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raghu is proud that his district ranks first in Karnataka for literacy and that both his sons can read and write fluently, something his own father could not do. He worries most about his livelihood: will private buses survive against free government transport, and what work will he find when his knees give out? He resents the Shakti scheme not because he opposes helping women but because it was introduced without compensating private operators, and he sees it as a political gimmick rather than genuine care. He blames the central government's fuel taxes for petrol crossing one hundred rupees per litre and the state government for failing to defend small transport workers. Raghu wants Tejas to study further and escape manual work, but he is resigned to the possibility that financial reality will cut that dream short, just as it did for Kiran. He admires Gulf-returned families who build concrete houses and start businesses, and he sees Kiran's recruitment-agency job as the family's one plausible path toward that prosperity. He fears illness and accident more than unemployment, knowing a single hospital stay could erase years of savings. He is uncomfortable with the communal rhetoric he hears from some passengers and colleagues but keeps his opinions to himself, believing politics and religion are best left unspoken on a bus. He is proud of Dakshina Kannada's Yakshagana and Bhuta Kola traditions and dislikes being told by outsiders that his region is defined only by moral policing and tension.
